issues.claim: for an `int` hole, as here, since C# 10 on .NET 6 and later versions it may use `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`, which formats the `int` without boxing
issues.problem: The fetched excerpt of the cited handler tutorial covers custom handlers and the handler pattern. It never mentions `DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler`, formatting without boxing, or the C# 10 / .NET 6 default behaviour. The claim is true from my own knowledge, and the conclusion that E allocates a new string is correct, but the cited page does not demonstrably support it. The same unsure was raised in round 1 and the repair only partly resolved it.
issues.suggestedFix: Replace or supplement links[3] with https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.defaultinterpolatedstringhandler (and re-title the link, e.g. 'DefaultInterpolatedStringHandler'). Alternatively, keep the tutorial link but drop the boxing detail so the claim is only 'the compiler may use a string.Concat or a handler; either way the result is a new string'.

issues.claim: The lambda captures no locals and no `this`, so the compiler caches the delegate in a static field of a hidden class.
issues.problem: The lambda-expressions excerpt does not show either the capture-of-outer-variables material or the compiler caching of non-capturing lambdas. Static-field caching is Roslyn implementation behaviour, not documented language semantics, and the repair notes themselves say so. The claim is correct for current Roslyn, but no cited page supports it. The page title 'captured outer variables' is also not confirmed by the excerpt.
issues.suggestedFix: Hedge the wording as implementation behaviour: 'the Roslyn compiler typically caches the delegate in a static field of a hidden class (an implementation detail, not a language guarantee)'. Cite the lambda page only for the capture claim (captured outer variables stay alive as long as the delegate). Optionally drop the 'static field' detail and say 'a non-capturing lambda does not need a closure object and its delegate is reused'.
